messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 58

# The Weight of a Moment

Martin is a 62-year-old man who has worked as a bank teller for nearly three decades. He is the kind of man who takes quiet pride in precision — in balanced ledgers, in remembering the names of regular customers, in doing things right. His wife, Elaine, describes him as steady, the sort of person you could set your watch by. That steadiness shattered fourteen months ago on a Saturday afternoon in his own driveway.

Martin had been backing his car out of the garage when his seven-year-old grandson, Tobias, ran behind the vehicle chasing a football. Martin did not see him. He felt the bump before he heard the scream. Tobias sustained a fractured pelvis and a broken femur, spending three weeks in hospital and months in rehabilitation. He has since made a strong physical recovery. Martin has not.

In the immediate aftermath, Martin moved through the necessary motions — calling the ambulance, riding to the hospital, sitting in waiting rooms — in a state he describes as "somewhere else entirely." He remembers the fluorescent lights of the emergency department with a vividness that still startles him. He remembers a nurse's blue lanyard. He remembers almost nothing else from those first days, as though his mind had simply refused to record them.

The nightmares began within the first week. He dreams of the moment of impact, though in his dreams Tobias does not survive. He wakes gasping, sometimes shouting, and lies rigid in the dark beside Elaine, unable to tell her what he has seen. He has stopped sleeping in their bed on nights when the dreams feel close, retreating to the couch so that she will not be disturbed. She is disturbed anyway.

At work, Martin functions — just. He counts notes, processes transactions, greets customers by name. But the bank has a car park visible through the front windows, and whenever he sees someone reversing, his chest tightens and his hands go cold. He has developed a habit of looking away, pretending to sort papers. A colleague once commented that he seemed distracted, and Martin felt a flush of shame so acute it took his breath away.

He has stopped driving whenever possible. When he must drive, he asks Elaine to walk ahead of the car and confirm the path is clear, a ritual she performs without complaint, though both of them know it has grown from something reasonable into something that governs their lives. He will not drive with children in or near the vehicle under any circumstances. He has not seen Tobias since a brief, stilted Christmas visit, which he ended early, telling Elaine he felt unwell. He had not felt unwell. He had felt that he did not deserve to be in the same room as the boy.

That belief — that he is a danger, that he is fundamentally careless despite a lifetime of carefulness — sits at the centre of everything. Martin does not frame it as guilt in any ordinary sense. He frames it as evidence. He has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him: checking and rechecking before he moves through any space, scanning for hazards, lying awake cataloguing the ways things can go wrong. He has lost nearly eight kilograms. He drinks more than he used to, two or three whiskies most evenings, which he tells himself is simply a habit and which Elaine has started to watch with a careful, worried expression he recognises and cannot bear.

He agreed to come to therapy, he says, because Elaine asked him to and because he could not think of a reason to refuse that did not sound like an excuse. He sits in the chair with his hands folded in his lap, very still, very controlled, and speaks about that Saturday afternoon in a flat, measured voice — the voice of a man who has told himself the story so many times he has learned to tell it without flinching. His eyes, however, tell a different story entirely.
